rules.title: FTP exposed
rules.explanation: FTP sends usernames, passwords, and files in clear text, so anyone on the network can read them.
rules.remediation: Disable FTP. Use SFTP or SCP (over SSH) for file transfer instead.

rules.title: SSH remote access available
rules.explanation: SSH is encrypted and generally safe, but an exposed SSH port can be brute-forced if it allows password login.
rules.remediation: Prefer key-based authentication, disable root login, and consider a tool like fail2ban.

rules.title: Telnet exposed
rules.explanation: Telnet transmits everything, including your password, in plain text and has no meaningful security. It is obsolete.
rules.remediation: Disable Telnet immediately and use SSH (port 22) for remote access.

rules.title: SMTP mail service exposed
rules.explanation: An open mail (SMTP) port on a home network is unusual and, if misconfigured, can be abused to relay spam.
rules.remediation: If you are not intentionally running a mail server, disable this service.

rules.title: DNS service present
rules.explanation: Port 53 (DNS) is normal on a router or a Pi-hole style device. Informational unless this host should not be a DNS server.
rules.remediation: No action needed if this is your router or DNS server.

rules.title: Unencrypted web service (HTTP)
rules.explanation: HTTP traffic, including any admin login, is unencrypted and can be read on the local network. Common on device admin panels.
rules.remediation: Use HTTPS where possible, and ensure any admin panel has a strong password.

rules.title: Plain-text mail retrieval (POP3)
rules.explanation: POP3 retrieves mail without encryption, exposing credentials and messages on the network.
rules.remediation: Use POP3S (995) or IMAPS (993) instead, or disable if unused.

rules.title: RPC portmapper exposed
rules.explanation: rpcbind can reveal available RPC services and has been abused in reflection/amplification attacks.
rules.remediation: Restrict or disable rpcbind if you are not using NFS or other RPC services.

rules.title: Windows RPC exposed
rules.explanation: Microsoft RPC (135) exposes Windows services and is a frequent target on unpatched systems.
rules.remediation: Block port 135 from untrusted networks at the firewall and keep Windows updated.

rules.title: Legacy NetBIOS exposed
rules.explanation: NetBIOS session service is legacy Windows file/printer sharing and can leak host information.
rules.remediation: Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP if not required; prefer SMB over 445 with modern settings.

rules.title: Plain-text mail access (IMAP)
rules.explanation: IMAP without TLS exposes mailbox credentials and contents on the network.
rules.remediation: Use IMAPS (993) instead, or disable if unused.

rules.title: Encrypted web service (HTTPS)
rules.explanation: HTTPS is the secure form of web traffic. Informational — this is generally what you want.
rules.remediation: No action needed. Ensure the certificate and admin password are sound.

rules.title: SMB file sharing exposed
rules.explanation: SMB (445) has a long history of wormable, critical vulnerabilities (e.g. EternalBlue) when exposed or unpatched.
rules.remediation: Restrict SMB to trusted hosts, disable SMBv1, and keep systems patched.

rules.title: Encrypted mail access (IMAPS)
rules.explanation: IMAP over TLS is the secure form of mail access. Informational.
rules.remediation: No action needed.

rules.title: Encrypted mail retrieval (POP3S)
rules.explanation: POP3 over TLS is the secure form of mail retrieval. Informational.
rules.remediation: No action needed.

rules.title: Insecure VPN (PPTP)
rules.explanation: PPTP VPN uses broken encryption and is considered unsafe.
rules.remediation: Disable PPTP and use a modern VPN such as WireGuard or OpenVPN.

rules.title: Database reachable on the network (MySQL)
rules.explanation: A database port open to the LAN lets other devices attempt to connect to or attack your data.
rules.remediation: Bind MySQL to localhost or restrict it by firewall; never expose databases to the general network.

rules.title: Remote Desktop exposed (RDP)
rules.explanation: RDP is a top target for brute-force and exploit attacks when reachable on the network.
rules.remediation: Restrict RDP to trusted hosts or a VPN, enable Network Level Authentication, and use strong passwords.

rules.title: Remote desktop exposed (VNC)
rules.explanation: VNC is often unencrypted and weakly authenticated, potentially exposing full control of the machine.
rules.remediation: Tunnel VNC over SSH or a VPN, require a strong password, or disable it.

rules.title: Unencrypted web service (HTTP 8080)
rules.explanation: Port 8080 commonly hosts an unencrypted web app or admin console readable on the LAN.
rules.remediation: Use HTTPS and a strong password, or restrict access to this service.
